newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Hungary's Goncz plays down impact of Cluj protests.
newsitem.headline: Hungary's Goncz plays down impact of Cluj protests.

text.p: Nationalist protests against the opening of a Hungarian consulate in the Romanian city of Cluj will not harm relations between the two states, Hungarian President Arpad Goncz said on Saturday.
Police on Wednesday thwarted the second attempt in as many weeks to seize a Hungarian flag from the newly-opened consulate.
"They will not have any influence. The world will not change overnight and even earlier we had to anticipate the appearance of such events," Goncz told a news conference in the Czech capital.

The foreign ministers of the two countries reopened the consulate, shut down by communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu in 1988, in July. The move was seen as a sign of further consolidation of relations between the two states.
In the first protest, the flag was snatched from the consulate by three men later found to be Cluj city employees.
But Goncz, visiting Prague to address central European students, said there would be no implications for relations as the Hungarian state was not the target of the demonstrations.
He said good relations between Romania and Hungary were in the interests of both countries and added, "This is something which is not dependent on the flag."

Romania is home to 1.6 million ethnic Hungarians, most of whom live in the Transylvania region around Cluj. But the city's mayor, Gheorghe Funar, has antagonised Hungarians by curbing their linguistic and cultural rights.

Goncz visited Romania in May -- the first visit by a Hungarian head of state in 70 years -- and vowed with Romanian President Emil Constantinescu to prevent nationalist extremists from undermining reconciliation.
Goncz said thousands of people had turned out to support the two presidents. "They are fed up with hatred," he said.
Romania and Hungary signed a treaty last year intended to help resolve disputes and pave the way for their accession to the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation and the European Union.
Hungary is among the three central European countries invited to join NATO and the five with which the EU plans to begin membership talks. Romania missed out on both.

Goncz said cooperation between the three successful NATO applicants, Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic, were good and that Budapest wanted similar cooperation with Romania and Slovenia, which also missed the first enlargement wave.
The president said Hungary was also prepared to cooperate with Slovakia, home to a 500,000-strong Hungarian minority.
"We would be ready to express the same towards Slovakia because the membership of Slovakia in the NATO alliance and the European Union is also in the national interest," he said.
Ties with Slovakia have been troubled by the treatment of the Hungarian minority. The two countries' prime ministers are to meet on August 15 in Gyor, Hungary.
